rationale: A wins because it stays inside the evidence fence and makes the missing proof painfully clear. A's "Allbirds says its new sugarcane-and-wool shoe outlasts the original wool runner — now it has to prove it" has the right skeptical posture; B's "Allbirds swaps wool for a sugarcane blend it says will finally make its shoes last" misstates the material and starts drinking the company's punch. B has a useful markets frame in "IPO-day math," but it pads into a sector trend it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "store closures plus a 40% product-range cut producing the first quarter of gross-margin improvement" overstates causality. The update says those things happened under the turnaround plan, not that the cuts produced the margin improvement.

"Can one good quarter win back investors holding Allbirds below its IPO price?" is refused as a duplicate, but the public-market credibility angle is stronger than A admits. It could be a real retail/markets lane, not just a footnote inside operations.
"Story type: category-creation" is the wrong label for the product angle. One company saying a blend is more durable is a materials-claim story, not a category story.
gaps_in_B: "DTC brands are shrinking to survive" is a trend claim the update does not supply. That needs outside comparables before it belongs in the headline, not after it.
"Allbirds swaps wool for a sugarcane blend" is factually sloppy. The update says the platform uses a sugarcane-and-wool blend, not that Allbirds swapped wool out.
"will finally make its shoes last" overbuys Allbirds' durability claim. The facts only say the company says it is more durable than the original wool runner.

"brands are choosing fewer, better bets over growth-at-all-costs" is tidy consultant wallpaper unless B brings actual sector evidence. As written, it is the kind of sentence that feels true because it sounds familiar.
